blocks.text: A motorcycle engine barrel is cast with deep fins because air alone cannot carry away the heat from a smooth cylinder. Yet on a thin electrical cable, adding a thin layer of insulation can make a small wire lose more heat and run cooler, not hotter. Both effects come from the same idea: how surface area interacts with a convection resistance.

blocks.markdown: A convective film resists heat flow with $R=1/(hA)$. When $h$ is low (gases, natural convection) the film is the bottleneck, and the cure is to raise the surface area $A$. An **extended surface**, or fin, does this by sticking metal out into the fluid. Heat conducts along the fin and is lost from its sides, so the fin is cooler toward its tip, and the added surface is not fully effective.

blocks.title: Fin parameter and fin equation
blocks.text: For a fin of uniform cross-section area $A_c$ (m$^2$) and perimeter $P$ (m), with conductivity $k$ and convection coefficient $h$, the parameter $m=\sqrt{hP/(kA_c)}$ (m$^{-1}$) sets how fast the excess temperature $\theta=T-T_\infty$ decays along the fin. Energy balance on a slice gives $d^2\theta/dx^2=m^2\theta$.

blocks.caption: Straight fin of uniform section, length L, base excess temperature theta_b = T_b - T_inf, steady, constant k and h

blocks.markdown: Two measures judge a fin. **Efficiency** $\eta_f=q_f/(hA_f\theta_b)$ compares it with an ideal fin that is everywhere at the base temperature, where $A_f$ is the fin surface area. **Effectiveness** $\varepsilon_f=q_f/(hA_c\theta_b)$ compares it with leaving the bare base area uncovered. For an adiabatic tip, $\eta_f=\tanh(mL)/(mL)$.

blocks.title: Straight rectangular fin with adiabatic tip
blocks.prompt: An aluminium rectangular fin ($k=200$ W/m K, typical) is 3 mm thick, 100 mm wide and 40 mm long, and is attached to a surface at 120 $^\circ$C. Air at 25 $^\circ$C gives $h=25$ W/m$^2$K. Treat the tip as adiabatic. Find the heat transfer, the fin efficiency and the fin effectiveness.

steps.text: Geometry: cross-section $A_c=wt=0.1\times0.003=3.0e-04$ m$^2$; perimeter $P=2(w+t)=0.206$ m (the small tip area is absorbed in the adiabatic-tip assumption).
Efficiency compares with an isothermal fin: $q_{max}=hP L\theta_b=19.6$ W, so $\eta=18.7/19.6=0.957$ (also $\tanh(mL)/(mL)$).
Effectiveness compares with the bare base: $\varepsilon=q/(hA_c\theta_b)=18.7/(25.0\times3.0e-04\times95)=26.3$.

blocks.answer: $q\approx18.7$ W, $\eta\approx0.96$, $\varepsilon\approx26$. The fin is well worthwhile since $\varepsilon\gg2$.

rows: Large $m$: heat dies out quickly along fin
Between 0 and 1; high for short, high-$k$ fins
Fins worthwhile if $\varepsilon_f\gg1$ (rule of thumb above 2)
blocks.caption: Summary of fin and insulation formulae

blocks.markdown: A fin is most useful where $h$ is small and $k$ is large. Making the fin longer helps only up to $mL\approx3$, because $\tanh(mL)\to1$ and the far part is nearly at the fluid temperature. Fins also add weight and cost, so a designer chooses a limited fin length rather than very long fins.

Insulation behaves differently on small cylinders. Adding insulation adds conduction resistance $\ln(r_2/r_1)/(2\pi k)$ but also raises the outer surface area, which cuts the film resistance $1/(2\pi r_2h)$. For a thin cylinder the film term can fall faster than the conduction term rises, so total resistance first falls, reaching a minimum when $r_2=r_{cr}=k/h$. Past that, further insulation does reduce the loss.

blocks.caption: Critical insulation radius of a cylinder (for a sphere, r_cr = 2k/h)

blocks.title: Insulation that increases heat loss
blocks.prompt: A small hot tube of outer radius 5 mm has a surface temperature of 80 $^\circ$C and loses heat to air at 20 $^\circ$C with $h=10$ W/m$^2$K. A plastic insulation with $k=0.2$ W/m K (typical) is added to outer radius $r_2$. Compare the heat loss per metre for the bare tube and for $r_2=10$, 20 and 40 mm. Assume $h$ is unchanged and the tube surface stays at 80 $^\circ$C.

steps.text: For a cylinder with insulation out to radius $r_2$ the resistance per metre is conduction in the insulation plus the outer film.
Critical radius: $r_{cr}=k/h=0.2/10=20$ mm. This is larger than the tube radius, so insulation up to about 20 mm will raise the loss.
Evaluate the loss with $q'=2\pi\Delta T/\left[\ln(r_2/r_1)/k+1/(hr_2)\right]$: $r_2=10$ mm gives 28.00 W/m; $r_2=20$ mm gives 31.60 W/m; $r_2=40$ mm gives 29.23 W/m.

Interpretation: the loss rises above the bare value, peaks at $r_2=r_{cr}$, and only falls below the bare value once the insulation radius is large enough (the third value is still above the bare value here, since the insulation must exceed roughly the break-even radius).

blocks.answer: Bare 18.85 W/m; with insulation 28.00, 31.60, 29.23 W/m at 10, 20 and 40 mm. All three are above the bare tube, and the maximum is at $r_{cr}=20$ mm.

blocks.title: Insulation can make things worse
blocks.text: If the bare outer radius $r_1<r_{cr}=k/h$, adding insulation raises heat loss until $r_2=r_{cr}$, and insulation must exceed a break-even radius before it beats the bare tube. Large pipes ($r_1>k/h$) always gain from insulation. This matters for electrical cables and small tubes, where it can be an advantage for cooling.

blocks.title: Fins in practice
blocks.text: Fins pay off on the low-$h$ side of a heat exchanger (gas side). Efficiency falls as $h$ rises or $k$ falls, and a fin whose effectiveness is below about 2 is probably not worth its cost.

points: A fin with adiabatic tip transfers $q_f=\sqrt{hPkA_c}\,\theta_b\tanh(mL)$ with $m=\sqrt{hP/(kA_c)}$.
Efficiency is $\tanh(mL)/(mL)$; effectiveness is $q_f/(hA_c\theta_b)$ and should be much greater than 1.
Fins help where $h$ is low and $k$ is high; length beyond $mL\approx3$ adds little.
Critical insulation radius of a cylinder is $r_{cr}=k/h$; below it, insulation increases heat loss.

questions.stem: A designer wants to add straight fins to a surface. Fin effectiveness $\varepsilon_f$ is defined as the ratio of

options.text: fin heat transfer to the heat from an ideal fin at the base temperature
heat from the fin tip to heat from the base
fin heat transfer to the heat transferred through the same base area without the fin
the base temperature to the ambient temperature

questions.correctOptionText: fin heat transfer to the heat transferred through the same base area without the fin

distractorRationale.a: This is fin efficiency, not effectiveness.
distractorRationale.b: This is not a standard definition; tip loss is a part of the fin heat transfer.
distractorRationale.d: This is a temperature ratio and has no energy meaning.

questions.explanation: Effectiveness answers the practical question of how much the fin improves on a bare base: $\varepsilon_f=q_f/(hA_c\theta_b)$. Efficiency compares against an ideal isothermal fin of the same surface area instead.

questions.stem: A thin electrical conductor of radius 2 mm is to be coated with plastic of conductivity $k=0.18$ W/m K, typical, in room air with $h=9$ W/m$^2$K. Calculate the critical insulation radius and state whether a coating of outer radius 12 mm will increase or decrease the heat loss compared with the bare conductor, giving reasons.
markingGuide: Bare radius (2 mm) is below the critical radius, so the heat loss increases as insulation is added until $r_2=20$ mm.
A 12 mm outer radius is still below $r_{cr}$, so the loss is higher than the bare conductor.
Reason: the outer area growth lowers the convective resistance faster than the conduction resistance rises.
questions.explanation: With $r_{cr}=20$ mm, a 12 mm outer radius lies on the rising part of the heat-loss curve, so the coating raises the loss and keeps the wire cooler. This is exactly why thin wires can be coated without penalising current rating.

questions.stem: A circular aluminium pin fin ($k=200$ W/m K, typical) of diameter 6 mm and length 50 mm projects from a wall at 100 $^\circ$C into air at 20 $^\circ$C with $h=40$ W/m$^2$K. Assume an adiabatic tip. Find the heat transfer from the fin in W.
questions.explanation: With $P=\pi D=0.01885$ m and $A_c=\pi D^2/4=2.827e-05$ m$^2$, $m=\sqrt{hP/(kA_c)}=11.55$ m$^{-1}$ and $mL=0.577$. Then $q=\sqrt{hPkA_c}\theta_b\tanh(mL)=0.06530\times80\times0.5207=2.720$ W.

questions.stem: A fin has $m=22$ m$^{-1}$ and length $L=50$ mm with an adiabatic tip. Find its efficiency $\eta_f=\tanh(mL)/(mL)$. Give the answer as a dimensionless number between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: $mL=22\times0.05=1.1$ and $\tanh(1.1)=0.8005$, so $\eta_f=0.8005/1.1=0.728$. A value near 0.7 means the fin is somewhat cooler toward the tip, so it delivers about 70% of the ideal.

questions.stem: A steam trace line is to be wrapped in rubber insulation of $k=0.35$ W/m K (typical) in still air with $h=9$ W/m$^2$K. Calculate the critical insulation radius in mm.
questions.explanation: For a cylinder $r_{cr}=k/h=0.35/9=0.0389$ m $=38.9$ mm. Insulation thinner than that on a smaller tube would increase the loss, while larger tubes gain from any insulation.

questions.stem: Two fins have identical geometry and the same convection coefficient, one made of copper and one of stainless steel, both with an adiabatic tip. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The steel fin has the higher efficiency because a lower $k$ keeps heat near the base
The copper fin has the higher efficiency because a larger $k$ gives a smaller $m$ and a flatter temperature profile
Efficiency is independent of $k$ and depends only on $h$
Both have the same efficiency but copper has larger effectiveness

questions.correctOptionText: The copper fin has the higher efficiency because a larger $k$ gives a smaller $m$ and a flatter temperature profile

distractorRationale.a: Low $k$ makes $m$ larger and the fin cooler toward the tip, lowering efficiency.
distractorRationale.c: Efficiency $\tanh(mL)/(mL)$ depends on $m=\sqrt{hP/kA_c}$, so on $k$ too.
distractorRationale.d: Effectiveness depends on $\eta$, so they differ in both measures.

questions.explanation: Since $m\propto1/\sqrt k$, a larger $k$ reduces $mL$ and brings $\tanh(mL)/(mL)$ closer to 1. The copper fin stays hotter toward the tip and so transfers more heat.

questions.stem: A long fin has $m=7$ m$^{-1}$ and adiabatic-tip behaviour. Its length is doubled from 0.35 m to 0.70 m with the same base temperature. What is the approximate change in heat transfer?

options.text: It doubles, as the surface area doubles
It decreases, as the longer fin has more resistance

distractorRationale.a: The far part of the fin is almost at ambient and carries little heat.
distractorRationale.b: The tanh factor changes by under 2%, not 50%.
distractorRationale.c: Heat transfer cannot decrease with a longer fin with fixed $h$; it saturates.

questions.explanation: With $mL$ going from 2.45 to 4.9, $\tanh$ rises from 0.985 to 0.9999, an increase of about 1.5%. Beyond $mL\approx3$ a longer fin is wasted metal.

questions.stem: Explain why adding a layer of insulation to a pipe can increase the heat loss, state the condition in terms of $k$, $h$ and the pipe radius, and say whether the effect matters for a 150 mm diameter steam main.
markingGuide: Two competing effects: extra conduction resistance $\ln(r_2/r_1)/(2\pi k)$ and a lower outer film resistance $1/(2\pi r_2 h)$ because surface area increases.
Total resistance has a minimum at $r_2=r_{cr}=k/h$, so heat loss is maximum there.
Insulation increases loss if the bare radius is below $k/h$ (and must be thick enough to pass the break-even radius to help).
For a 150 mm main, $r_1=75$ mm is far greater than a typical $r_{cr}$ (for example $k=0.05$, $h=10$ gives 5 mm), so insulation always reduces the loss.
questions.explanation: The answer rests on the derivative of total resistance with respect to $r_2$. For ordinary pipes and lagging, $k/h$ is millimetres, so the effect only matters for thin wires and small tubes.

questions.stem: A heat exchanger has water on one side ($h\approx1500$ W/m$^2$K) and air on the other ($h\approx40$ W/m$^2$K). On which side should fins be attached, and why? Use the effectiveness criterion in your answer.
markingGuide: Fins go on the air side, where $h$ is low.
Effectiveness $\varepsilon_f=q_f/(hA_c\theta_b)$ is large when $h$ is small because the bare surface is a poor heat remover and the fin adds area where it matters.
On the water side, the large $h$ makes the bare surface already effective and the fin efficiency drops because $m$ is large, so $\varepsilon_f$ is small.
Fins on the air side reduce the dominant thermal resistance in the overall resistance chain.
questions.explanation: Fins reduce the largest resistance in series. The air film $1/(hA)$ is about 40 times that of water, so adding area there gives most of the improvement.

questions.stem: A bare tube of outer radius 5 mm at 80 $^\circ$C loses heat to 20 $^\circ$C air with $h=10$ W/m$^2$K. It is then wrapped in insulation of $k=0.2$ W/m K up to an outer radius of 20 mm. Taking the surface temperature of the tube as fixed, find the ratio of the heat loss with the insulation to that of the bare tube (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Bare: $q'=2\pi(0.005)(10)(60)=18.85$ W/m. Insulated: $q'=2\pi(60)/[\ln(4)/0.2+1/(10\times0.02)]=376.99/(6.9315+5)=31.60$ W/m. The ratio is 1.676, meaning 20 mm radius sits exactly at $r_{cr}=k/h=20$ mm where the loss is a maximum (about 68% more than bare).
